title: The World of AI: AI Courses catalogue in Research and Learning
answer: The World of AI publishes this AI Courses catalogue within its Research and Learning section. It lists courses with level, audience, cost and a verified source, and says it tracks 13 AI courses, 11 free, 3 with companion code, re-verified daily. Its most useful point is the split between university graduate courses, described as exam-driven theory, and industry courses, described as code-first or hands-on, so the choice is about learning style rather than which source is more rigorous. The page also notes it does not report enrollment or completion rates.

sections.body: The World of AI publishes this page as part of its AI Research and Learning section, within its wider AI ecosystem. It is a catalogue of AI courses rather than a report or study. The page gives each course a level, an intended audience, cost information and a verified source, and it states that source links are re-verified daily. The page carries a last verified date of 2026-09-26. It says membership is editorial, based on significance rather than sponsorship, and that nothing is paid placement. The supplied text also includes promotional material for books, consulting services and a novel at the bottom, which sits outside the course catalogue itself.
sections.heading: What this source is

sections.body: The page says it covers 13 AI courses, 11 free, with 3 having public companion code, curated by level and audience and with one verified source each. It describes university and platform courses with duration, cost and what they teach. DeepLearning.AI on Coursera appears at beginner level for managers, executives and anyone working alongside technical teams, free to audit with a certificate fee. A second DeepLearning.AI course is intermediate, for people after the ML Specialization, free to audit with a paid certificate. Dataquest is beginner level for developers wanting hands-on practice with LLM APIs, by subscription. fast.ai is beginner to intermediate for programmers and top-down learners, free, with companion code. DeepLearning.AI and Stanford on Coursera is beginner level, described as the first course for most people, free to audit with a paid certificate. The text then says all ten courses tracked offer free access to core materials, though three, DeepLearning.AI's specializations and Karpathy's and fast.ai's courses, pair that with a paid certificate option or public code repositories. It says four are university graduate courses with public materials, Stanford's CS224n and CS231n, UC Berkeley's CS285 and MIT's 6.S191, while the rest come from industry, DeepLearning.AI, Google, Hugging Face, fast.ai and Andrej Karpathy. It argues university courses are generally exam-driven theory while industry courses are code-first or hands-on, so the choice is about learning style rather than rigour. Only three list public code, fast.ai, Karpathy's Zero to Hero and MIT's 6.S191. The data does not report enrollment, completion or popularity.
sections.heading: What it says

sections.body: The page states 13 AI courses, 11 free and 3 with public companion code, re-verified daily, with a last verified date of 2026-09-26. It later says all ten courses tracked offer free access to core materials, and refers to these ten, so the top-line count of 13 does not match the later count of ten. It lists five course entries in the supplied text. It says four are university graduate courses, Stanford's CS224n and CS231n, UC Berkeley's CS285 and MIT's 6.S191, and that only three list public code, fast.ai, Karpathy's Zero to Hero and MIT's 6.S191. It states that membership is editorial, significance not sponsorship, and nothing is paid placement. It also states the data does not report enrollment numbers, completion rates or which of these ten is most widely taken. Costs given include free to audit with certificate fee, paid certificate, subscription and free.
sections.heading: Figures and claims worth noting

sections.body: A reader following AI in Education can use this source as a directory of AI courses, not as evidence about their outcomes. It helps compare options by level, audience, cost and free access, and it highlights the divide between university graduate courses and industry courses. That divide is useful for curriculum design, professional development or advising learners, because it frames the choice as learning style rather than prestige. The page also points to an AI Skills Graph, which suggests the courses are meant to map to skills, though the supplied text does not detail that mapping. It is a starting point for finding courses, and it is clear about what its data does not measure.
sections.heading: What it means for AI in Education

sections.body: The page is a catalogue, not a study, and it does not report enrollment, completion or popularity. Its counts are inconsistent in the supplied text, with 13 courses at the top and ten later, and only five entries shown. It does not cover certifications in detail, teaching quality, learner outcomes or employer recognition. It is dated by its last verified date of 2026-09-26, though it says links are re-verified daily. The page also carries promotional material for books, consulting services and a novel, so despite the editorial membership claim it is not purely neutral. It is partial and should be checked against the live page.
